messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Painter
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 34

He describes the day the sky cracks open, though he never gives the exact date. It is always just “before” and “after.” At thirty-two, he stands in the middle of a schoolhouse, rolling white latex over cinderblocks. The sirens start like distant trains. Then the ground jumps. When the dust settles, the roof is gone. His brushes lie under splintered wood and something that is not quite red, not quite brown. He digs them out before he lets himself look at the floor. He always digs things out before he lets himself look at the floor. He leaves six months later with his wife, carrying a duffel of bristles, a half-empty can of primer, and the quiet terror of watching his neighborhood fold into rubble. For years, he keeps moving. Construction jobs, then framing, then finally residential painting in this quiet suburb where the walls are thick and the traffic moves slowly enough to predict. He tells me his hands never really learn how to stay still after the explosions. Even now, at fifty-three, they carry a low hum, a tightness in the knuckles that only loosens when he loads a drop cloth into his truck or watches the sun hit a freshly coated ceiling. He comes to our Tuesday sessions wearing the same gray cardigan. When he describes the sound of a backfiring car, his shoulders rise toward his ears and his breath catches in a way that feels borrowed. He checks the windows twice before they begin, not because he is anxious, but because he needs to map the exits in his head the way his father once taught him to check the gas lines. He does not remember the last time he sleeps through the night without waking at 2:14 a.m., the exact hour the sirens used to cut off. When his wife touches his shoulder unexpectedly, he flinches before he smiles. He loves her, he says, but the love feels like a room he visits rather than lives in. Some days, he watches her sleep and wonders when the silence becomes so heavy. On weekends, he paints. He works on a client’s sunroom, rolling paint in steady, parallel strokes. The smell of the thinner usually brings it back—the metallic tang, the sudden drop in his stomach, the way the dust motes arrange themselves into the shapes of collapsed eaves. He pauses, steps outside, and breathes until his vision clears. He tells me he does not mind the work anymore. The walls are predictable. They hold what he puts on them. But lately, when he climbs the ladder, his hands hesitate. The rungs feel like scaffolding. He lowers himself down and drinks water until the tightness behind his ribs uncoils. He walks his daughter to her car after their sessions, hands deep in his pockets, eyes tracking the streetlights as they flicker on. He tells me he is trying to be present, to notice the color of his wife’s scarf, the way the neighbors’ dog barks at the mail carrier, the steady rhythm of his own breathing. He says he does not want to lose himself again. He does not say what happens when he does, but I see it in the way his jaw tightens when a delivery truck reverses too close, in the careful way he folds his hands on his lap, in the quiet hope that maybe, one day, the ground will stop feeling like it is waiting to jump.
